ox: Wrong. This swaps the electrodes. Oxidation never happens at the cathode, and electrons do not flow from cathode to anode.
Wrong. Reduction happens at the cathode, not the anode. The direction anode to cathode is right but the label is wrong.
Wrong. Reduction at the cathode is right, but electrons flow from anode to cathode. The direction is reversed.
Correct. Oxidation at the anode frees electrons. They travel through the wire to the cathode, where a species is reduced.

p: A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to make electricity. Oxidation (losing electrons) happens at the anode. Reduction (gaining electrons) happens at the cathode.
Electrons always move from the anode to the cathode through the wire.

mem: Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode (always)
Electrons flow anode to cathode
In a galvanic cell, the anode is negative and the cathode is positive
d_4C_1.mn: An Ox and Red Cat: Anode = Oxidation, Reduction = Cathode. Also, LEO the lion says GER: Lose Electrons Oxidation, Gain Electrons Reduction.
d_4C_1.trap: Mixing up electron flow with conventional current, which runs the opposite way.
d_4C_1.plain: Electrons are like kids leaving a crowded room (anode) through a hallway (wire) to an empty room (cathode).

ox: Correct. Charging uses an outside power source to force the nonspontaneous reverse reaction. That makes the cell electrolytic.
Wrong. A galvanic cell is spontaneous and cannot be recharged just by swapping electrodes. Charging needs an external power source.
Wrong. A concentration cell runs on a concentration difference. Charging a battery reverses its chemistry, not a gradient.
Wrong. A fuel cell is continually fed fresh reactants. It is not a battery being recharged.

p: A galvanic cell releases energy from a spontaneous reaction, like a battery discharging. An electrolytic cell uses outside energy to force a nonspontaneous reaction.
A rechargeable battery is galvanic when it discharges and electrolytic when it charges.

mem: Discharging = galvanic (spontaneous, delta G < 0)
Charging = electrolytic (nonspontaneous, needs power source)
Cathode is still where reduction occurs in both
d_4C_11.trap: Thinking the cell stays galvanic while charging.
d_4C_11.plain: A ball rolling downhill makes energy by itself (discharge). Pushing it back uphill takes your effort (charging).

ox: Wrong. This reverses it. The 1.0 M half-cell is the cathode, where Cu2+ is reduced to lower its concentration.
Correct. The dilute 0.1 M side is the anode. Cu is oxidized there, adding Cu2+ to raise its concentration. Electrons flow from 0.1 M to 1.0 M.
Wrong. Standard E0 is zero, but the cell potential also depends on Q through the Nernst equation. Different concentrations give a nonzero E.
Wrong. Electrons flow from anode to cathode, so this is backward.

p: A concentration cell has the same metal and ion on both sides but at different concentrations. The cell tries to even them out.
The dilute side gains ions (oxidation, anode). The concentrated side loses ions (reduction, cathode). Electrons go from anode to cathode.

mem: Dilute side = anode; concentrated side = cathode
E0cell = 0 but E is greater than 0 when concentrations differ
Cell runs until concentrations are equal
d_4C_12.trap: Seeing E0 = 0 and concluding no current.
d_4C_12.plain: Two cups of juice, one strong and one weak. Nature moves flavor from strong to weak. Here, the weak cup gets more stuff added and the strong cup gets thinned out.

ox: Wrong. This doubles E0, treating it like an extensive quantity such as delta G. Potential does not scale.
Wrong. Halving E0 is also not how potentials behave. Coefficients do not change E0.
Wrong. Flipping the sign applies only when you reverse the half-reaction, not when you multiply it.
Correct. Reduction potential is intensive (independent of amount). Multiplying coefficients does not change E0, so it stays +0.80 V.

p: An intensive property does not depend on how much material you have. Reduction potential is intensive, a measure of electron-pulling strength per electron.
Extensive properties like delta G (energy) do scale with the amount, because more electrons move.

mem: E0 does not change when you multiply a half-reaction
Reversing a half-reaction flips the sign of E0
delta G = -nFE scales with n
d_4C_14.trap: Scaling E0 with coefficients as though it were delta G.
d_4C_14.plain: A strong magnet is just as strong whether you have one or two. Two magnets together hold more weight, but each is no stronger.

ox: Correct. In molten NaCl, Na+ is reduced to Na(l) at the cathode, and Cl- is oxidized to Cl2 gas at the anode.
Wrong. This swaps electrodes. Cations are reduced at the cathode and anions oxidized at the anode, never the reverse.
Wrong. H2 needs water, which is absent in a molten salt. Only the Cl2 part is right.
Wrong. O2 would need water. With only Na+ and Cl- present, chloride is oxidized to Cl2.

p: In electrolysis, an outside power source forces a reaction. A molten salt has only its own ions, no water. So the cation is reduced at the cathode and the anion oxidized at the anode.
In aqueous solution, water can also react, which changes the products.

mem: Molten salt: only the salt's own ions react
Cation reduced at cathode; anion oxidized at anode
Aqueous solutions may give H2 or O2 from water
d_4C_15.trap: Using aqueous electrolysis products (H2, O2) for a molten salt.
d_4C_15.plain: With only two kinds of players on the field, each has to play its own position. No substitutes (water) are available.

ox: Wrong. Voltage rises only if capacitance falls. A dielectric raises capacitance, so voltage goes down.
Wrong. With no battery attached, no charge can enter. Charge stays fixed.
Correct. Q is fixed because the capacitor is isolated. The dielectric raises C by kappa, so V = Q/C falls.
Wrong. Charge has nowhere to go on an isolated capacitor, so it stays constant.

p: A capacitor stores charge (Q) on two plates. Capacitance (C) tells how much charge it holds per volt: C = Q/V. A dielectric is an insulating material that raises capacitance by a factor kappa.
If the battery is disconnected, Q cannot change. If the battery stays connected, V stays fixed instead.

mem: Dielectric multiplies C by kappa
Disconnected: Q constant, V falls
Connected: V constant, Q rises

fm.f: V = Q/C, where V = voltage, Q = charge, C = capacitance
fm.v: Q fixed; C becomes kappa x C (kappa greater than 1)
fm.why: The isolated capacitor keeps Q, so V must fall as C rises.
fm.nc: Dividing by kappa just makes V smaller.

d_4C_23.trap: Assuming charge changes when the capacitor is isolated.
d_4C_23.plain: A sealed water balloon has a fixed amount of water. If you make the balloon bigger, the pressure inside drops.

ox: Wrong. This reverses the placements. An ammeter across a resistor is nearly a short circuit, and a voltmeter in series blocks current.
Wrong. A voltmeter in series has huge resistance and would block current, so it would not measure the resistor's voltage.
Wrong. An ammeter in parallel is almost a wire and would short the circuit, not measure the resistor's current.
Correct. A voltmeter measures a potential difference across two points, so it goes in parallel (high resistance). An ammeter measures current through a path, so it goes in series (low resistance).

p: Voltage is a difference between two points, so a voltmeter connects across the part, in parallel. It has very high resistance so it takes almost no current.
Current is flow through the wire, so an ammeter is placed in the path, in series. It has very low resistance so it does not change the current.

mem: Voltmeter: parallel, very high resistance
Ammeter: series, very low resistance
Wrong placement can short the circuit or block it
d_4C_26.mn: Amps in a Row (series), Volts Across (parallel).
d_4C_26.plain: To measure a hill's height, you compare top and bottom (across it). To count cars on a road, you stand on the road where all cars pass (in line).

ox: Correct. Conventional current is defined as the movement of positive charge, from positive to negative terminal. Electrons actually move the opposite way.
Wrong. This is the direction electrons move, not conventional current.
Wrong. Conventional current is opposite to electron flow, not the same.
Wrong. A battery gives direct current (DC) with a constant direction. Alternating current comes from AC sources.

p: Early scientists defined current as flow of positive charge, before electrons were discovered. This is conventional current, going from the positive to the negative terminal.
In metal wires, the real moving charges are electrons, which go from negative to positive.

mem: Conventional current: positive to negative
Electron flow: negative to positive
Battery gives DC; wall outlet gives AC
d_4C_34.trap: Equating conventional current with electron flow.
d_4C_34.plain: Imagine a line of kids moving left. You could say 'kids move left' or 'empty spaces move right.' Conventional current is like tracking the empty spaces.

ox: Wrong. Lower resistance means more current leaks out of the axon, which would slow conduction.
Wrong. Higher capacitance means the membrane takes more charge to change voltage, which slows conduction. Myelin lowers capacitance.
Wrong. Ion channels are packed at the nodes of Ranvier (gaps), not under the myelin sheath.
Correct. Myelin is insulation. It raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so less current leaks and less charge is needed to depolarize the next node. The signal jumps node to node.

p: Myelin is a fatty wrap around axons. Like insulation on a wire, it stops current from leaking out and makes the membrane thicker (lower capacitance).
The signal jumps between nodes of Ranvier, the gaps where ion channels sit. This jumping is called saltatory conduction.

mem: Myelin: resistance up, capacitance down
Ion channels cluster at nodes of Ranvier
Saltatory conduction means jumping between nodes
d_4C_37.plain: A garden hose with holes loses water. Wrapping tape around it keeps the water moving forward faster.

ox: Correct. The 6 and 3 ohm pair is 2 ohms, so total R = 6 ohms and I = 12/6 = 2 A. The 4 ohm resistor drops 8 V, leaving 4 V across the pair. I(6 ohm) = 4/6 = 0.67 A.

Wrong. 0.33 A does not match this circuit. Total current is 12 V / 6 ohm = 2 A, and it splits 2 : 1 between the 3 ohm and 6 ohm branches (the smaller resistor gets more). The 3 ohm branch carries about 1.33 A and the 6 ohm branch about 0.67 A. Trap: reading the 1/3 split fraction as a current.
Wrong. 1.33 A is the current through the 3 ohm branch (4/3). It is the wrong branch.
Wrong. 2.0 A is the total current, not the current in one branch.

p: Resistors in parallel combine as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Resistors in series just add. Total current splits among parallel branches.
Find total current first, subtract the series voltage drop, then use the leftover voltage across each parallel branch.

mem: Series: R adds; same current
Parallel: same voltage; currents add
Parallel 6 and 3 ohm gives (6 x 3)/(6 + 3) = 2 ohms

fm.f: Ohm's law: V = I x R, where V = voltage, I = current, R = resistance
fm.v: V = 12, parallel pair = 2 ohms, series resistor = 4 ohms
fm.why: Ohm's law applies to each part, with voltage shared as the circuit splits.

d_4C_40.sc: Currents split in inverse proportion to resistance. The 3 ohm branch gets 2/3 of the 2 A total and the 6 ohm branch gets 1/3 of 2 A, which is 2/3 A, about 0.67 A.
d_4C_40.trap: Giving the total current instead of the branch current.
d_4C_40.plain: Water flows through one big pipe, then splits into a narrow and a wide pipe. More water goes through the wide one.

ox: Wrong. This describes a galvanic cell. Also, oxidation never occurs at the cathode.
Wrong. Positive E0cell and negative delta G describe a spontaneous galvanic cell. Electrolytic cells are the opposite.
Wrong. Reduction occurs at the cathode in every cell. Only the sign of the electrode changes in an electrolytic cell, not its process.
Correct. An electrolytic cell uses an external power source to drive a nonspontaneous reaction (delta G > 0, E0cell < 0). Reduction still occurs at the cathode.

p: An electrolytic cell uses outside electrical energy to force a reaction that would not happen on its own. Its delta G is positive and its E0cell is negative.
Roles stay fixed: reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode. Only the signs flip: the cathode is negative and the anode is positive.

mem: Electrolytic: delta G > 0, E0cell < 0, needs power source
Reduction at cathode, oxidation at anode always
Galvanic: cathode positive; electrolytic: cathode negative
d_4C_5.mn: An Ox and Red Cat: Anode = Oxidation, Reduction = Cathode.
d_4C_5.trap: Assuming electrode roles flip in electrolytic cells. Only the signs flip.
d_4C_5.plain: Pushing a bike uphill takes your effort. The hill is still a hill; you are just working against it.

ox: Wrong. A positive delta G0 goes with a NEGATIVE E0, and K above 1 needs a negative delta G0. This option contradicts itself. The trap is flipping the sign in delta G0 = -nFE0.
Wrong. Negative delta G0 is right, but it means K is greater than 1, not less. The trap is forgetting that ln K has the same sign as E0.
Wrong. Positive delta G0 and K below 1 describe a nonspontaneous reaction, which needs a negative E0. The question says E0 is positive.
Correct. Positive E0 makes delta G0 = -nFE0 negative. Negative delta G0 = -RT ln K means ln K is positive, so K is greater than 1.

concept.t: Cell potential, free energy and K
p: E0 is the standard cell potential, the voltage a cell makes under standard conditions. Delta G0 is the standard free energy change. Negative delta G0 means the reaction is spontaneous (it runs on its own).
K is the equilibrium constant. If K is above 1, products are favored. The three are linked: delta G0 = -nFE0 = -RT ln K. A positive E0 means negative delta G0 and K above 1.

mem: E0 positive = delta G0 negative = K greater than 1 = spontaneous
E0 negative = delta G0 positive = K less than 1 = nonspontaneous
delta G0 = -nFE0 = -RT ln K

fm.f: delta G0 = -n F E0, where n = moles of electrons transferred, F = Faraday constant, E0 = standard cell potential, delta G0 = standard free energy change
fm.v: E0 is positive; n and F are always positive
fm.why: It links voltage to free energy, so the sign of E0 gives the sign of delta G0.
fm.nc: Only the sign matters, so no arithmetic is needed.

d_4C_9.trap: Mixing up the signs. The minus sign in delta G0 = -nFE0 flips positive E0 into negative delta G0.
d_4C_9.plain: Think of a ball rolling downhill. Positive E0 is a downhill slope, so the ball (the reaction) rolls toward products on its own.

ox: Wrong. 9 ohms is 6 + 3, the series formula. Parallel resistance must be smaller than the smallest branch.
Correct. 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohms. It is smaller than 3 ohms, as parallel resistance always is.
Wrong. 4.5 ohms is the average of 6 and 3. Parallel combinations are not averages; the result is always below the smallest resistor.
Wrong. 18 ohms is 6 x 3, the product alone. The product-over-sum rule needs the division by 9: 18/9 = 2.

p: Resistance (in ohms) measures how much a part opposes current. In parallel, current has several paths to choose from, like extra lanes on a road. More paths make it easier to flow, so the total resistance goes down.
Add the reciprocals: 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2. For two resistors you can also use product over sum.

mem: Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, and R is less than the smallest branch
Series: R = R1 + R2
Two resistors in parallel: R = (R1 x R2)/(R1 + R2)

fm.f: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, where R1 and R2 = the two resistors, R = equivalent resistance we solve for
fm.why: The resistors share the same two connection points, so they are in parallel.
fm.nc: Use a common denominator of 6, or product over sum: 18/9 = 2.

q53.sc: If one resistor is double the other, the answer is one third of the larger: 6/3 = 2.
q53.trap: Using the series formula (9), the average (4.5) or the product (18). Check that your answer is smaller than 3.
q53.plain: Imagine two doors to a room instead of one. More doors means people get through more easily, so the 'door resistance' drops.

ox: Correct. Capacitance is C = kappa x epsilon0 x A / d. Putting a dielectric in raises C by a factor of kappa.
Wrong. Dielectrics always raise capacitance because kappa is 1 or greater. Do not mix this up with a larger plate gap d, which lowers C.
Wrong. Capacitance depends on plate area, gap and the material between the plates. Changing the material changes C.
Wrong. kappa appears to the first power in the formula. Squaring is a trap from inverse-square laws like Coulomb's law.

p: A capacitor is two metal plates that store charge. Capacitance (C) measures how much charge it stores per volt. A dielectric is an insulating material placed between the plates.
The dielectric constant kappa says how much the material boosts capacitance. Vacuum has kappa = 1. Everything else is above 1, so C = kappa x C0.

mem: C = kappa x epsilon0 x A / d
Dielectric in: C goes up by kappa, kappa is at least 1
More area raises C; more gap lowers C

fm.f: C = kappa x epsilon0 x A / d, where kappa = dielectric constant, epsilon0 = permittivity of free space, A = plate area, d = plate separation, C = capacitance
fm.v: A, d and epsilon0 unchanged; only kappa is added
fm.s: C new = kappa x (epsilon0 A / d) = kappa x C old
fm.why: Only kappa changed, so C scales directly with it.
fm.nc: No numbers needed.

q54.trap: Choosing the inverse (decrease) or a square. The relationship is a simple linear multiplication by kappa.
q54.plain: A bigger backpack holds more books for the same effort. A dielectric is like a bigger backpack for charge.

ox: Correct. In a galvanic cell oxidation happens at the anode. Electrons leave the anode and travel through the wire to the cathode.
Wrong. Reduction happens at the cathode. Remember: Red Cat (reduction at the cathode).
Wrong. Electrons always flow from anode to cathode in every cell type. Reversing this is a common slip.
Wrong. A galvanic cell is spontaneous, so E0 cell is positive. Negative E0 cell describes an electrolytic cell.

p: A galvanic (voltaic) cell is a battery. A spontaneous redox reaction makes electricity. Oxidation (losing electrons) happens at the anode. Reduction (gaining electrons) happens at the cathode.
Electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode. E0 cell is positive and delta G is negative. An electrolytic cell is the opposite: it uses outside power to force a nonspontaneous reaction.

mem: Galvanic: spontaneous, E0 positive, delta G negative
Anode = oxidation; cathode = reduction (always)
Electrons flow anode to cathode
q55.mn: AN OX and RED CAT: ANode = OXidation, REDuction = CAThode. Also LEO says GER: Lose Electrons Oxidation, Gain Electrons Reduction.
q55.trap: Flipping anode and cathode, or thinking E0 can be negative in a galvanic cell.
q55.plain: Electrons are like kids sliding down a slide on their own. The anode is the top, the cathode is the bottom, and the kids move without being pushed.

ox: Correct. Ohm's law: I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A. Power P = IV = 3 x 12 = 36 W.
Wrong. 48 A comes from multiplying V by R. Ohm's law divides: I = V/R.
Wrong. 3 A is right, but 12 W uses V alone. Power needs both current and voltage: P = IV.
Wrong. 0.33 A is R divided by V (4/12). Ohm's law has V on top.

p: Voltage (V, in volts) is the push on the charges. Resistance (R, in ohms) is the opposition. Current (I, in amps) is the flow. Ohm's law says V = IR.
Power (P, in watts) is energy used per second. P = IV, which is also I squared times R, or V squared over R.

mem: V = IR so I = V/R
P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R
Watts = volts x amps

fm.f: I = V / R and P = I x V, where V = voltage, R = resistance, I = current, P = power
fm.why: The resistor is a simple ohmic load across the battery, so Ohm's law applies.

q56.trap: Multiplying instead of dividing in Ohm's law, or forgetting that power needs both I and V.
q56.plain: Water in a hose: voltage is how hard you push, the narrow hose is the resistance, and the water per second is the current.

ox: Correct. The positive rod pulls electrons toward the sphere. Grounding lets more electrons flow in from the earth. Removing the ground first traps them, so the sphere ends up negative.
Wrong. Induced charge by grounding is opposite to the rod. Positive would be the answer only if the rod were negative.
Wrong. The sphere would stay neutral only without grounding. Grounding while the rod is near lets net charge flow in.
Wrong. This describes polarization (charge shifting) with no grounding. Grounding adds actual net charge, so the sphere is not neutral.

p: Induction charges an object without touching it. A charged rod comes near a neutral conductor. Free electrons in the metal move toward or away from the rod.

Grounding connects the sphere to the earth, a huge reservoir of electrons. A positive rod pulls electrons in from ground. If you cut the ground first and then remove the rod, the extra electrons stay: the sphere is negative.

mem: Induction gives the opposite charge to the rod
Order: rod near, ground, remove ground, remove rod
Without grounding, you only get polarization with net charge still zero
x4C_006.mn: Order of steps: bring the rod, ground it, cut the ground, remove the rod.
x4C_006.trap: Answering neutral because charges only shift. Grounding is what changes net charge.
x4C_006.plain: A magnet-like friend stands nearby and calls kids over to your tent through a door (the ground). You close the door and the friend leaves. The kids stay in your tent.

ox: Wrong. The midpoint balances only equal charges. Here +4q pushes harder, so the zero point must be closer to the smaller charge.
Wrong. x = 2 m is closer to the +4q charge, which pushes harder there. The null point must be closer to +q.
Correct. Set q/x^2 = 4q/(3 - x)^2. Square roots give 1/x = 2/(3 - x), so 3 - x = 2x and x = 1 m.
Wrong. Left of +q, both charges push the test charge in the same direction (to the left). The forces add and never cancel.

concept.t: Force balance between two like charges
p: Coulomb's law says the force between charges is F = kq1q2/r^2. A test charge feels a push from each source. Two positive charges both push a positive test charge away.
Between them the pushes point opposite ways, so they can cancel. The stronger charge needs a larger distance to match, so the zero point sits closer to the weaker charge.

mem: Like charges: null point lies between them, closer to the smaller charge
Distance ratio = square root of charge ratio (4q vs q gives 2 : 1)
Outside the pair, forces add and cannot cancel

fm.f: kq1/x^2 = kq2/(d - x)^2, where q1 = q, q2 = 4q, x = distance from +q, d = 3 m total separation
fm.why: At the null point, the two repulsive forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
fm.nc: Square root of 4 is 2, so split 3 m in the ratio 1 : 2.

x4C_007.sc: Split the distance in the ratio 1 : sqrt(4) = 1 : 2, giving 1 m and 2 m.
x4C_007.trap: Picking the midpoint, or putting the point closer to the larger charge.
x4C_007.plain: Two kids on a seesaw: the heavier kid has to sit closer to the middle to balance. Here the stronger charge is 'farther' so the weaker one is 'closer'.

ox: Wrong. Each force does drop by a factor of 4, but they drop together, so their ratio does not change.
Wrong. Neither force gets stronger with distance, and neither shrinks more slowly than the other.
Wrong. Both forces follow 1/r^2, not 1/r. Even so, the ratio would not change.
Correct. Electric force kq^2/r^2 and gravity Gm^2/r^2 both scale as 1/r^2. The r^2 cancels in the ratio, so it stays about 10^36.

p: Coulomb's law (electric force) and Newton's law of gravitation both say force is proportional to 1 divided by distance squared. Double the distance and each force falls to one quarter.
If you divide one by the other, the distance terms cancel. The ratio depends only on charges and masses, not on how far apart the particles are.

mem: Coulomb: F = kq1q2/r^2; gravity: F = Gm1m2/r^2
Doubling r cuts each force to 1/4
Ratio of two inverse-square forces is independent of r

fm.f: Ratio = F electric / F gravity = (kq^2/r^2)/(Gm^2/r^2) = kq^2/(Gm^2), where k = Coulomb constant, G = gravitational constant, q = charge, m = mass, r = distance
fm.s: Both numerator and denominator are divided by 4, so the ratio is unchanged
fm.why: Both laws share the same r^2 dependence, so r cancels.
fm.nc: No numbers needed.

x4C_010.trap: Thinking that because forces shrink by 4, the ratio must also shrink by 4.
x4C_010.plain: Two flashlights dim the same way as you walk away. If one is always a billion times brighter, that gap stays the same at any distance.

ox: Wrong. Zero is the electric potential at the midpoint (a scalar that cancels). The field is a vector, and both contributions point the same way, so they add.
Wrong. 4kq/d^2 is only one charge's contribution. Both charges contribute at the midpoint, so you must add the two.
Correct. Each charge is d/2 away, so each gives kq/(d/2)^2 = 4kq/d^2. Both fields point toward -q, so the total is 8kq/d^2.
Wrong. This uses d instead of d/2 as the distance, and it gives the wrong magnitude. The midpoint is d/2 from each charge.

p: The electric field (E) shows the force per unit positive charge. It points away from positive charges and toward negative charges. Field magnitude from a point charge is E = kq/r^2, where r is the distance.
Fields are vectors, so direction matters. At the midpoint between +q and -q, both fields point toward -q. They add. Potential is a scalar, so it cancels there, but field does not.

mem: Field points away from +, toward -
Midpoint of a dipole: fields add (total = 2 x one field)
Potential is zero at the midpoint; field is not

fm.f: E = kq/r^2, where k = Coulomb constant, q = charge size, r = distance to the point
fm.why: Both fields point the same way at the midpoint, so we add.

x4C_015.trap: Answering zero by mixing up scalar potential with the vector field.
x4C_015.plain: Standing between a kid pushing you and a kid pulling you from the same side: both help you move the same way, so you feel double the effect.

ox: Wrong. Electric force is F = qE, which depends on charge, not mass. Proton and electron have the same size charge.
Correct. Both have |q| = e, so forces are equal in size (opposite direction). a = F/m, and the electron is about 1800 times lighter, so it accelerates far more.
Wrong. Forces are equal, but masses are very different, so accelerations are not equal.
Wrong. Particle size does not appear in F = qE. The charges have the same magnitude, so the forces are the same.

concept.t: Force and acceleration in an electric field
p: A charge q in an electric field E feels force F = qE. Positive charges are pushed along the field. Negative charges are pushed against it.
Acceleration comes from Newton's second law: a = F/m. If forces are equal, the lighter particle has the larger acceleration.

mem: F = qE; a = F/m
Proton and electron: equal charge size, opposite sign
Electron mass is about 1/1800 of proton mass

fm.f: a = qE/m, where q = charge, E = field strength, m = mass, a = acceleration
fm.v: q is equal in size for both; m electron is about 1/1800 of m proton
fm.s: a electron / a proton = m proton / m electron = about 1800
fm.why: Same force on a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration.
fm.nc: Only the ratio matters, so no calculation is needed.

x4C_017.trap: Thinking the heavier particle feels the bigger force. Mass changes acceleration, not the electric force.
x4C_017.plain: Two people get the same push, one a toddler and one a grown adult. The toddler zooms off faster because there is less weight to move.

ox: Wrong. A conductor does not let the field pass through. Its free charges move until the field inside is canceled.
Wrong. Induced charges oppose the external field. They do not reinforce it, so the field does not double.
Wrong. The net field is zero, not a reversed copy. The induced field cancels the external one exactly.
Correct. Free charges shift to the surface until their field cancels the external field inside. A closed conducting shell has zero field in its empty cavity (Faraday cage).

p: A conductor has electrons that move freely. In an external field they shift until their own field exactly cancels the outside field in the metal.
Once charges settle, the field inside is zero. For a hollow conductor with an empty cavity, the field inside the cavity is also zero. This is electrostatic shielding.

mem: Inside a conductor at equilibrium, E = 0
Excess charge sits on the outer surface
Hollow conductor shields its cavity (Faraday cage)
x4C_018.trap: Picking 'equal and opposite' because the induced field is opposite. The total, after adding both, is zero.
x4C_018.plain: A crowd of kids rushes to one side of a room until pushing is even all around. Anyone standing in the middle feels no push at all.

ox: Wrong. A negative charge in an upward field feels a downward force, adding to gravity instead of balancing it.
Wrong. 3.2 x 10^-19 C doubles the needed charge. Weight is only 1.6 x 10^-14 N, which needs one elementary charge.
Wrong. This is off by a power of ten. Dividing 1.6 x 10^-14 by 10^5 gives 1.6 x 10^-19, not 10^-20.
Correct. qE = mg gives q = (1.6 x 10^-15 x 10)/10^5 = 1.6 x 10^-19 C. The force must point up, along E, so the charge is positive.

p: A drop hangs still when net force is zero. Gravity pulls down with weight mg. The electric force qE must push up with equal strength.
A positive charge is pushed along the field direction. An upward field and an upward force means a positive charge. The elementary charge e is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.

mem: Hovering: qE = mg
Positive charge: force along E; negative: force opposite to E

fm.f: q E = m g, where q = charge, E = field, m = mass, g = gravity
fm.why: At rest, upward electric force equals downward weight.
fm.nc: Add exponents: -15 + 1 = -14, then -14 - 5 = -19.

x4C_019.trap: Ignoring the sign and picking a negative charge, or making a power-of-ten slip.
x4C_019.plain: A balloon floats still when its upward lift matches its downward weight. The electric push is the lift here.

ox: Correct. r = mv/(qB). With q, v and B equal, r is proportional to m. Double the mass, double the radius.
Wrong. Heavier ions are harder to turn, so the path is wider, not tighter.
Wrong. Radius depends on m to the first power. Squaring is a trap from kinetic energy or inverse-square formulas.
Wrong. Mass is in the radius formula, so it matters. Different masses are what the spectrometer separates.

concept.t: Circular motion in a magnetic field
p: A magnetic field pushes a moving charge sideways, so it moves in a circle. The magnetic force qvB acts as the centripetal force (the inward force needed to move in a circle), mv^2/r.
Setting them equal gives r = mv/(qB). A heavier ion has more momentum, so it makes a larger circle.

mem: r = mv/(qB)
r is proportional to m and v; inversely proportional to q and B
Mass spectrometers sort ions by mass-to-charge ratio

fm.f: qvB = mv^2/r so r = mv/(qB), where q = charge, v = speed, B = magnetic field, m = mass, r = radius
fm.v: q, v, B same; m2 = 2 x m1
fm.why: Magnetic force supplies the centripetal force for circular motion.
fm.nc: Just scale: double m, double r.

x4C_039.trap: Thinking heavier means less curving in the sense of tighter, or squaring the mass.
x4C_039.plain: A heavy truck takes a wider turn than a small car at the same speed with the same steering.

ox: Wrong. NaCl is a strong electrolyte but gives only 2 ions per formula unit (Na+ and Cl-), fewer than CaCl2.
Wrong. Acetic acid is a weak acid, so only a small fraction ionizes and few ions are made. Weak electrolytes conduct poorly.
Correct. CaCl2 dissociates fully into 3 ions (Ca2+ and 2 Cl-). At equal molarity it gives the most charge carriers and the best conductivity.
Wrong. Glucose dissolves as whole molecules, so there are no ions. It is a nonelectrolyte and conducts almost nothing.

p: Solutions conduct electricity through mobile ions (charged particles). An electrolyte is a substance that makes ions in water. Strong electrolytes fully split into ions. Weak ones only partly. Nonelectrolytes make none.
At the same concentration, more ions per formula unit and higher ion charge means better conduction. CaCl2 makes three ions, NaCl two.

mem: Conductivity rises with ion count and ion charge
Strong electrolytes (salts, strong acids) beat weak ones
Sugars like glucose are nonelectrolytes
x4C_053.trap: Picking NaCl because it is the familiar salt. Count the ions: CaCl2 gives 3, NaCl gives 2.
x4C_053.plain: Ions are like kids carrying buckets of water down a line. More kids means more water gets passed along. Glucose has no kids at all.

ox: Wrong. This flips the relationship. The same current through a smaller area needs faster electrons, not slower.
Correct. I = nqAv_d. With n, q and I fixed, v_d is proportional to 1/A. Halving the area doubles the drift speed.
Wrong. v_d depends on 1/A, not 1/A^2. Halving A gives a factor of 2, not 4.
Wrong. If the speed stayed the same, a smaller area would carry less current. To keep the same I, speed must increase.

p: Drift speed (v_d) is the slow average speed of electrons moving along a wire. Current (I) is charge flowing per second. The formula is I = nqAv_d, where n is the number of carriers per volume, q is charge of each, and A is the cross-sectional area.
If I and n are fixed, a smaller area forces the electrons to move faster to carry the same amount per second.

mem: I = nqAv_d
Same current: v_d is proportional to 1/A
Same metal means same n

fm.f: I = n q A v_d, where I = current, n = carrier density, q = carrier charge, A = cross-sectional area, v_d = drift speed
fm.v: I, n, q same; A_B = A_A/2
fm.s: v_d(B) = I/(nq A_B) = I/(nq A_A/2) = 2 x v_d(A)
fm.why: Same current through half the area needs double the speed.
fm.nc: Dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by 2.

x4C_055.trap: Picking 'half as fast' by assuming smaller wire means smaller flow. Current is held fixed.
x4C_055.plain: Cars on a road squeeze into one lane: to move the same number of cars per minute through the narrow lane, they must drive faster.

ox: Wrong. 3 A is the total current from the battery. It splits between the two parallel branches.
Wrong. 2 A is the current through the 6 ohm branch (12 V / 6). The 12 ohm branch carries less.
Wrong. This splits 3 A equally. Parallel branches share the same voltage, not the same current.
Correct. The parallel pair is (6 x 12)/18 = 4 ohms. Total is 4 + 4 = 8 ohms, I = 24/8 = 3 A. Series 4 ohm drops 12 V, leaving 12 V across the pair, so 12/12 = 1 A.

p: Reduce the circuit step by step. Find the equivalent resistance of the parallel part, add it to the series part, then find the total current with Ohm's law (V = IR).
Series resistors split the voltage. Parallel branches share the same voltage, but current splits, with more going through the smaller resistance.

mem: Series: same current, voltages add
Parallel: same voltage, currents add
Smaller resistor takes more current

fm.f: R parallel = (R1 x R2)/(R1 + R2); I = V/R; V across pair = V battery - I x R series; I branch = V across pair / R branch
fm.s: R pair = 72/18 = 4; R total = 8; I = 24/8 = 3 A; V series = 3 x 4 = 12 V; V pair = 24 - 12 = 12 V; I(12 ohm) = 12/12 = 1 A
fm.why: Parallel branches share voltage, so each branch current is V pair divided by its resistance.
fm.nc: The pair equals the series resistor (4 ohms), so the battery splits 12 V and 12 V.

x4C_060.sc: Currents in parallel split in inverse ratio of resistance: 6 : 12 is 2 : 1, so 3 A splits 2 A and 1 A.
x4C_060.trap: Splitting current equally between branches, or stopping at the total current.
x4C_060.plain: A road splits into a wide lane and a narrow lane. Both lanes start and end at the same places, but more cars take the wide one.

ox: Wrong. The terminal voltage equals the emf only when no current flows. Here 3 A flows, so some voltage is lost inside the battery.
Correct. Current is I = 9/(2+1) = 3 A. The battery loses Ir = 3 V inside, so the terminal voltage is 9 - 3 = 6 V. This also equals IR across the 2 ohm load: 3 x 2 = 6 V.
Wrong. 3 V is the voltage lost across the internal resistance (Ir = 3 x 1), not the voltage at the terminals. This is the 'lost' voltage, so you answered the wrong piece.
Wrong. This comes from using I = 9/2 = 4.5 A and ignoring the internal resistance. The current must include both resistances in series.

concept.t: Terminal voltage of a real battery
p: A real battery has a small resistance inside it, called internal resistance (r). The emf is the voltage the battery makes. The terminal voltage is what you actually get at its two ends when current flows.
Current flows through r and the outside resistor R in series: I = emf/(R + r). Some voltage is used up inside: Ir. Terminal voltage = emf - Ir.

mem: Terminal voltage V = emf - Ir
Current uses total resistance: I = emf/(R + r)
V equals emf only when I = 0
Terminal voltage also equals IR of the external load

fm.f: I = emf/(R + r) and V = emf - Ir, where emf = battery voltage, R = external resistance, r = internal resistance, I = current, V = terminal voltage
fm.v: emf = 9 V, R = 2 ohm, r = 1 ohm
fm.why: The internal and external resistors are in series, so the same current passes through both.
fm.nc: 9/3 = 3 and 3 x 1 = 3 are easy by hand.

x4C_066.sc: Series voltage divider: the terminal voltage is the fraction R/(R + r) of the emf. Here 2/3 of 9 V = 6 V.
x4C_066.trap: Forgetting the internal resistance in the current (I = 9/2) or reporting the lost voltage (3 V) as the answer.
x4C_066.plain: A water slide has a bumpy start. Some of your speed is lost before you reach the pool. The battery loses some voltage inside before it reaches the outside.

ox: Wrong. One-fourth is the series-type reasoning backward. In parallel the smaller resistor gets more power, not less.
Wrong. Equal voltage does not mean equal power. Power also depends on resistance, and the resistors are different.
Wrong. The resistance ratio is 4, so the power ratio is 4, not 2. Using a square root or halving the ratio is a mistake.
Correct. Parallel resistors have the same voltage V. Power P = V^2/R, so power is inversely proportional to R. The 2 ohm resistor has 1/4 the resistance, so it gets 4 times the power.

p: In a parallel circuit, every branch has the same voltage across it. Power is the rate energy turns into heat. When voltage V is fixed, power P = V^2/R.
A smaller resistance lets more current through at the same voltage, so it burns more power. In series it is the opposite: the current is the same, and P = I^2R, so the bigger resistor gets more.

mem: Parallel: same V, use P = V^2/R
Series: same I, use P = I^2R
Parallel: smallest R gets the most power
Series: largest R gets the most power

fm.f: P = V^2/R, where P = power, V = voltage across the resistor, R = resistance
fm.v: R1 = 2 ohm, R2 = 8 ohm, same V
fm.why: The voltage is shared by both parallel branches, so V cancels in the ratio.
fm.nc: Just divide 8 by 2. No need to know V.

x4C_073.sc: Parallel: power ratio is the inverse of the resistance ratio. Series: power ratio equals the resistance ratio.
x4C_073.trap: Using the series rule (P = I^2R) in a parallel circuit, which flips the answer to one-fourth.
x4C_073.plain: Two slides side by side with the same height. The wide, easy slide lets many kids through, so more kids use it. The small resistor is the wide slide.

ox: Wrong. Loss depends on current squared (I^2R), not current. Halving I gives a quarter, not a half.
Wrong. This comes from using V^2/R with the whole transmission voltage. That voltage is not the voltage across the wire. Higher V actually means lower loss.
Correct. For fixed power P = IV, doubling V halves I. Heat loss in the line is I^2R, so (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of the old loss.
Wrong. The loss does change because the current changes. Power delivered stays the same, but the current in the wires drops.

p: Power delivered equals current times voltage, P = IV. If P stays fixed and V goes up, the current I must go down.
Wires have a small resistance R. Heat lost in the wire is P = I^2R. Because current is squared, a small drop in current gives a large drop in loss. This is why power companies use very high voltage.

mem: P = IV, so higher V means lower I for the same P
Line loss = I^2 R_line
Double V, current halves, loss falls to 1/4
Use the current and the line resistance, not the full voltage

fm.f: P_loss = I^2 R, where I = current in the line, R = line resistance; and I = P/V
fm.s: I_new = P/(2V) = I/2; loss_new = (I/2)^2 R = (1/4) I^2 R
fm.why: The wire loss depends on the current through the wire.

x4C_075.sc: Loss goes as 1/V^2 at fixed delivered power. Double V, loss is 1/4.
x4C_075.trap: Plugging the transmission voltage into V^2/R. That is not the voltage across the line.
x4C_075.plain: Carrying water in fewer, bigger buckets means fewer trips and less spilling. High voltage means less current, so less heat is wasted.

ox: Correct. The battery holds V fixed. Doubling d halves C (C = e0 A/d). Q = CV, so Q halves, and charge flows back to the battery.
Wrong. Charge stays constant only if the capacitor is disconnected. Here the battery is attached, so it holds V, and Q can change.
Wrong. Pulling the plates apart lowers C, not raises it. A lower C at the same V means less charge.
Wrong. C is proportional to 1/d, so doubling d halves C. Squaring the change gives 1/4, which is wrong.

p: A capacitor stores charge Q on its plates. Capacitance C tells how much charge it holds per volt: Q = CV. For parallel plates, C = e0 A/d, where A is plate area and d is the gap.
If a battery stays connected, it keeps the voltage V constant. Change d, and C changes, so Q = CV changes.

mem: Battery connected: V is constant
Battery disconnected: Q is constant
C = e0 A/d, so C goes as 1/d
Q = CV

fm.f: Q = CV and C = e0 A/d, where Q = charge, C = capacitance, V = voltage, A = plate area, d = separation, e0 = a constant
fm.why: The battery fixes V, so Q must follow C.
fm.nc: Only a factor of 2 is involved.

x4C_081.sc: First ask: battery on or off? On means V fixed. Off means Q fixed.
x4C_081.trap: Assuming charge is always constant. It is constant only for an isolated capacitor.
x4C_081.plain: A battery is a pump holding the water level fixed. Make the bucket smaller and it simply holds less water at that same level.

ox: Wrong. Energy halves only if the voltage is held constant (U = 1/2 CV^2 with C halved). Here the battery is disconnected, so Q is fixed instead.
Wrong. Energy does change. You must do work to pull apart plates that attract each other, and that work is stored as extra energy.
Correct. Q is fixed. Doubling d halves C. U = Q^2/(2C), so halving C doubles U. The extra energy is the work you did pulling the plates apart.
Wrong. U goes as 1/C, and C only halves, so U doubles. Squaring the change again gives 4, which is the mistake.

p: When a capacitor is disconnected, its charge Q cannot leave, so Q stays fixed. Energy stored is U = Q^2/(2C).
Pulling the plates apart makes C smaller (C = e0 A/d). With Q fixed and C smaller, U gets larger. The plates attract, so pulling takes work, which becomes stored energy.

mem: Disconnected: Q fixed
U = Q^2/(2C) when Q is fixed
U = 1/2 CV^2 when V is fixed
Double d: C halves

fm.f: U = Q^2/(2C), where U = stored energy, Q = charge, C = capacitance
fm.why: Charge is fixed, so use the form of U that has Q in it.
fm.nc: Dividing by C/2 is the same as multiplying by 2.

x4C_082.sc: Q fixed: U goes as 1/C. Halve C, double U.
x4C_082.trap: Using U = 1/2 CV^2 and forgetting that V changes when the battery is gone.
x4C_082.plain: Pulling two magnets apart takes effort. You put that effort into the system, so it holds more energy.

ox: Wrong. U rises by kappa only if the battery stays connected and V is fixed (U = 1/2 CV^2). Here the battery is disconnected, so Q is fixed.
Wrong. C changes (it goes up by kappa), and with Q fixed, U = Q^2/(2C) must change.
Wrong. U depends on 1/C, and C changes by kappa only, so U changes by kappa, not kappa squared.
Correct. Q is fixed. The dielectric multiplies C by kappa. U = Q^2/(2C), so U drops to 1/kappa of its old value.

p: A dielectric is an insulating material put between the plates. It multiplies the capacitance by its dielectric constant, kappa (kappa is greater than 1).
If the capacitor is disconnected, Q stays fixed. Energy U = Q^2/(2C). A bigger C means less stored energy, so U goes down by a factor of kappa. The voltage also drops by kappa.

mem: Disconnected: Q fixed
Dielectric: C goes up by kappa
Isolated + dielectric: V and U both fall by kappa
Connected + dielectric: V fixed, Q and U rise by kappa

fm.f: U = Q^2/(2C), where Q = charge, C = capacitance, kappa = dielectric constant
fm.why: The charge is fixed, so the form with Q is the right one.
fm.nc: Just divide by kappa.

x4C_085.sc: Ask if the battery is on or off. Off: Q fixed and U goes as 1/C.
x4C_085.trap: Using U = 1/2 CV^2 with V fixed, which gives the battery-connected answer.
x4C_085.plain: A bigger bucket holding the same amount of water has a lower water level. The dielectric makes the bucket bigger, so the 'level' (voltage and energy) drops.

ox: Wrong. A dielectric is an insulator. If it conducted, charge would pass between the plates and the capacitor would be shorted out.
Correct. The dielectric's molecules polarize and line up, making an opposing field. This lowers the net field and the voltage for a given charge, so C = Q/V goes up by kappa.
Wrong. A dielectric does not add free electrons. The charge on the plates is the same; the polarization only changes the field.
Wrong. C = e0 A/d does depend on area, but a dielectric does not change the plate area. It works by polarization.

p: A dielectric is an insulator. In an electric field its molecules stretch or turn so that one side is slightly positive and the other slightly negative. This is called polarization.
This sets up a small field that points against the plates' field. The net field is smaller, so the voltage needed for the same charge is smaller. Since C = Q/V, capacitance goes up by kappa.

mem: Dielectric = insulator that polarizes
Polarization field opposes the plates' field
Net field and V drop at fixed Q
C = Q/V rises by kappa
x4C_090.sc: Remember: dielectric means insulator, so any answer with conduction or free charges is out.
x4C_090.trap: Thinking the dielectric conducts or changes the plate area. It changes the field inside the gap.
x4C_090.plain: Imagine a crowd pushing you forward, but a few friends push gently back. The net push is weaker. The dielectric 'pushes back' on the plates' field.

ox: Wrong. The anode is negative in a galvanic cell. In an electrolytic cell the signs flip, and this is the common mix-up.
Wrong. The external power source gives each electrode a definite charge. Neither electrode is neutral.
Correct. The external source pulls electrons out of the anode, making it positive. The cathode is pushed full of electrons, so it is negative.
Wrong. The sign does not depend on the metal. In an electrolytic cell the anode is always positive.

p: An electrolytic cell uses an outside power source to force a reaction that would not happen by itself. The anode is where oxidation happens (loss of electrons). The cathode is where reduction happens (gain of electrons).
The power source pulls electrons away from the anode, so it is positive. It pushes electrons onto the cathode, so it is negative. In a galvanic cell the signs are reversed.

mem: Oxidation always happens at the anode
Electrolytic: anode (+), cathode (-)
Galvanic: anode (-), cathode (+)
Electrons flow anode to cathode in both
x4C_094.mn: AN OX and RED CAT: ANode = OXidation, REDuction = CAThode. Also, 'EPA': Electrolytic Positive Anode.
x4C_094.trap: Memorizing 'anode is negative' from galvanic cells and applying it to electrolytic cells.
x4C_094.plain: A charger forces a battery to go backward. It pulls electrons off one side and pushes them onto the other, so the signs are the opposite of normal.

ox: Wrong. Cations move toward the cathode. Anions go the other way, toward the anode.
Correct. Metal cations form at the anode, building up positive charge there. Anions from the salt bridge move to the anode compartment to cancel it.
Wrong. Both anions and cations in the salt bridge move. Each is needed to keep both compartments neutral.
Wrong. Ions cannot travel through a metal wire. Only electrons move in the wire.

p: A salt bridge is a tube of salt solution joining the two half-cells. It lets ions move so the circuit is complete and each side stays electrically neutral.
At the anode, metal is oxidized into positive ions, so positive charge builds up. Anions move in to balance it. At the cathode, positive ions are used up, so cations move in.

mem: Anions move toward the anode
Cations move toward the cathode
Electrons travel only in the wire
Salt bridge keeps neutrality and completes the circuit
x4C_095.mn: AN ION to the AN ODE: ANions go to the ANode. CAThodes attract CATions.
x4C_095.trap: Mixing up which way ions go, or thinking ions travel in the wire.
x4C_095.plain: Think of a see-saw of charge. When one side gets too many positives, negatives walk over to even it out.

ox: Correct. Water is much easier to reduce than Na+. At the cathode, 2H2O + 2e- gives H2 gas + 2OH-.
Wrong. Sodium metal forms only from molten NaCl. In water, Na+ has a very negative reduction potential, so water is reduced first.
Wrong. Chlorine gas is made by oxidation of Cl-. Oxidation happens at the anode, not the cathode.
Wrong. Oxygen could come from oxidizing water, which is an anode process. The cathode is where reduction happens.

p: In electrolysis, the cathode reduces whichever species is easiest to reduce. The easiest is the one with the highest (least negative) reduction potential.
In aqueous NaCl, water can be reduced to H2 gas and OH- much more easily than Na+ can become sodium metal. So H2 bubbles at the cathode. Cl2 forms at the anode, and the solution becomes basic.

mem: Cathode = reduction
Aqueous NaCl: H2 at cathode, Cl2 at anode
Molten NaCl: Na metal at cathode
Very reactive metal ions (Na+, K+) are not reduced in water
x4C_100.trap: Predicting sodium metal. That is only true for molten NaCl with no water present.
x4C_100.plain: Two kids want to take the same toy. The easier one gets it first. Water is easier to reduce than sodium, so water wins.

ox: Correct. At the cathode, cations like Cu2+ are used up, leaving extra negative charge. K+ moves into that compartment to restore neutrality.
Wrong. Moving toward the anode is the path of NO3-, the anion. Cations move to the cathode.
Wrong. Ions do not travel through the metal wire. Only electrons do.
Wrong. Both ions move. K+ and NO3- both migrate to keep each half-cell neutral.

concept.t: Which way ions move in a salt bridge
p: In a galvanic cell, cathode ions like Cu2+ are reduced and removed from solution. This leaves extra negative charge there.
Positive K+ ions from the salt bridge move into the cathode compartment to cancel it. Negative NO3- ions move toward the anode compartment, where positive ions are being made.

mem: Cations (K+) go to the cathode
Anions (NO3-) go to the anode
Only electrons travel in the wire
Salt bridge ions must not react with the half-cell ions
x4C_104.mn: CATions go to the CATHODE; ANions go to the ANODE.
x4C_104.trap: Reversing the directions or thinking the ions use the external wire.
x4C_104.plain: If one room loses its positive kids, positive kids walk in from the hallway to even things out.

ox: Wrong. This adds the magnitudes (1.66 + 0.25). Cell potential is a difference of potentials, not a sum.
Wrong. This divides by 3 because of three electrons. E is intensive; it does not scale with electron number.
Wrong. This doubles the value for stoichiometry. Potentials are never multiplied by coefficients.
Correct. Ni2+ has the higher E(red), so it is the cathode. E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode) = -0.25 - (-1.66) = +1.41 V.

p: E(red) says how much a species wants to gain electrons. The half-reaction with the higher E(red) is reduced (the cathode). The other is oxidized (the anode).
E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode), using the reduction potentials as given. Do not multiply by coefficients. A positive E(cell) means the cell is spontaneous (galvanic).

mem: E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode)
Higher E(red) is the cathode
Never multiply E by coefficients
E(cell) positive means spontaneous

fm.f: E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode), where all E are standard reduction potentials in volts
fm.why: Cell voltage is the difference between the two reduction potentials.
fm.nc: 1.66 - 0.25 = 1.41 by simple subtraction.

x4C_113.sc: Subtract the smaller from the larger. The answer should be positive for a galvanic cell.
x4C_113.trap: Adding potentials or scaling by the number of electrons.
x4C_113.plain: Two kids pulling a rope for electrons. The stronger puller wins, and the score is how much stronger.

ox: Wrong. A positive value would mean M is reduced more easily than H+, so M would be the cathode. But M is the anode.
Wrong. This divides by 2 for two electrons. Potentials do not scale with electron number.
Correct. SHE is the cathode (E = 0). E(cell) = 0 - E(M) = +0.44, so E(M) = -0.44 V.
Wrong. This doubles the value for two electrons. E is intensive and not multiplied.

concept.t: Finding E(red) from a cell with SHE
p: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is the reference with E(red) = 0 V. In a cell, E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode).
If M is the anode, SHE is the cathode. So 0.44 = 0 - E(M). A metal that is oxidized by H+ must have a negative reduction potential.

mem: SHE has E = 0.00 V
E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode)
Anode partner of SHE has negative E(red)
Do not scale E by n

fm.f: E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode), where E(cathode) = 0 for SHE
fm.why: M is the anode, SHE is the cathode.
fm.nc: One subtraction with 0.

x4C_116.sc: M is the anode and the cell is positive, so M must be below 0 on the table.
x4C_116.trap: Giving +0.44 V by forgetting the minus sign for the anode term.
x4C_116.plain: Hydrogen is sea level. A metal that sits below sea level (negative) gives up its electrons to hydrogen.

ox: Wrong. This applies n = 2 but does not square [H+] in Q. The H+ term is squared, which cancels the 2 in the exponent and the 1/2 out front.
Correct. pH 1 vs pH 4 is a 10^3 difference in [H+]. For H+ the voltage is 0.06 V per decade, so 0.06 x 3 = 0.18 V.
Wrong. This adds the pH values (1 + 4 = 5 decades). You must subtract: 4 - 1 = 3 decades.
Wrong. 0 V is E(standard) for identical cells. A concentration cell gives voltage when concentrations differ.

p: A concentration cell has the same electrodes but different concentrations. It makes voltage as the concentrations try to even out. The standard voltage is 0 V.
Nernst at 25 C: E = (0.06/n) log(Q), where n = electrons and Q is the ratio. For H+, Q has [H+] squared and n = 2, so E = 0.06 per decade of [H+] difference.

mem: Concentration cell: E(standard) = 0
Nernst at 25 C: E = (0.06/n) log Q
Each pH unit of difference gives 0.06 V for the H+ cell
Subtract pH values, do not add them

fm.f: E = 0.06 x (pH difference), where E = cell voltage in volts, pH difference = larger pH minus smaller pH
fm.why: The ratio is 10^3, so log = 3, and the 2 from n cancels with the squared H+.

x4C_125.sc: For H2 electrodes: voltage = 0.06 V x pH difference.
x4C_125.trap: Adding the pH values or forgetting that [H+] is squared in Q.
x4C_125.plain: Two tanks of water at different levels. The bigger the level difference, the harder the water flows. A bigger concentration difference gives more voltage.

ox: Wrong. Adding voltages to 3.0 V is what series connection does. Parallel cells share the same two terminals.
Wrong. Identical parallel sources do not divide voltage. Each still supplies 1.5 V.
Correct. Parallel cells share the same terminals, so voltage stays 1.5 V. The load current is split between them, so the pair lasts about twice as long.
Wrong. Parallel does not add voltage. Only series adds voltage.

p: Cells in series are connected end to end. Their voltages add, but the same current flows through each, so the run time is about the same.
Cells in parallel are connected terminal to terminal. The voltage stays the same as one cell. Each cell supplies only part of the current, so the pair lasts longer (more capacity).

mem: Series: voltages add, capacity same
Parallel: voltage same, capacity adds
Identical cells in parallel share current equally
Parallel doubles run time for two cells

fm.f: V_total = V (parallel) and run time = (number of cells) x (one-cell run time), where V = voltage of one cell
fm.s: V = 1.5 V; run time = 2 x one cell
fm.why: Parallel cells share both terminals, and the load current splits between them.

x4C_131.trap: Thinking parallel adds voltage. It adds capacity, not voltage.
x4C_131.plain: Two people carrying the same bucket handle: the bucket is not any higher, but each person gets less tired. Parallel cells give the same voltage but last longer.

ox: Wrong. O2 is reduced at the cathode. Oxidation of H2 happens at the anode. Oxidation is always at the anode, but the species oxidized is H2.
Wrong. A fuel cell is a galvanic cell. Its reaction is spontaneous and it makes electricity. It does not need an external source.
Correct. A fuel cell is fed H2 and O2 continuously from outside, so it runs as long as fuel is supplied. An ordinary battery has its reactants sealed inside.
Wrong. In all galvanic cells, electrons flow from the anode to the cathode, so this is not a difference.

p: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell: a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity. At the anode H2 is oxidized. At the cathode O2 is reduced, forming water.
The key difference from an ordinary battery is that the reactants are supplied continuously from outside. A normal battery has a fixed amount of reactants inside and goes dead when they are used up.

mem: Fuel cell = galvanic cell
H2 oxidized at anode, O2 reduced at cathode
Reactants fed in continuously
Electrons flow anode to cathode
x4C_134.trap: Thinking fuel cells need electricity to run (that is electrolysis) or mixing up which gas is oxidized.
x4C_134.plain: A normal battery is a water bottle that runs out. A fuel cell is a bottle with a hose to a tap, so it keeps going.
